newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cargo concerns for bridge link to new HK airport.
newsitem.headline: Cargo concerns for bridge link to new HK airport.

text.p: The world's second longest suspension bridge is due to be officially opened this weekend amid concern among Hong Kong's air cargo industry about the "unthinkable", industry sources told Reuters.
The HK$7.1 billion, eight lane, double-deck road and rail bridge is the spectacular centre piece of the Lantau link which includes two other bridges and viaducts. It will open for traffic on May 22.

It is the only land connection between the territory's new Chek Lap Kok airport off Lantau island and the rest of Hong Kong. Industry sources fear if the link were ever cut, the airport would be paralysed and Hong Kong's economy immediately affected.
Cargo sources said last year's Channel Tunnel fire showed how disaster can easily strike and cause months of chaos for cargo operators.

Security concerns at the new bridge were raised earlier this week when electrical wires were cut in 32 places. Already tight security has been strengthened, according to officials. A barge derrick crashing into a nearby bridge last year also raised safety concerns.

A Hong Kong government spokesman said the chances of the bridge ever having to close were "very very remote." He said it was typhoon-proof and road traffic could switch to the enclosed lower deck but said "unforeseen things can happen." A private company has been given the contract to ensure traffic flows smoothly along the entire Tsing Ma control area, he added.

In the event of the "worst case scenario" with a total bridge closure, the spokesman said contingency measures are being drawn up for passenger ferries to be requisitioned and replace the express rail service which will also use the bridge. As yet, there are no provisions for cargo handling. "If the worst comes to the worst, passengers are the priority. We have no contingency plan for cargo yet" he said in an interview.

With Hong Kong handling record amounts of cargo up to 5,700 tonnes in one day, it is doubtful whether any contingency measures would be able to handle just a fraction of the daily total, industry sources said.

Yeung Kwok Keung, deputy managing director of Hong Kong Air Cargo Terminals Ltd which will operate the SuperTerminal One air cargo terminal at Chek Lap Kok, said this week's wire cutting sabotage had been helpful in raising security concerns.

"It does not bear thinking about that the airport operation will be reliant on anything other than the bridge link. If in the unlikely, unwelcome and unfortunate event of the link being cut off and with the sea-based contingency plan in operation, I have no doubt whatsoever that the impact on flight movements will be very significant," Yeung told Reuters.

With thousands of consignments being handled every day, the terminal would quickly clog up with incoming cargo and run out of storage space. Aircraft bound for Hong Kong would then have to be turned away and departing flights could leave empty, Yeung said.

"The cargo industry has to look at and consider the likely impact on their trade of such a long cut off and it is something which we will be looking at. It is a general concern but we are not terrified as yet at the prospect of such a disconnection because we do believe that the possibility is low to the extreme," Yeung added.
An Airline Operators Committee source, which represents all airlines, airport managers and ground handling managers said he is also concerned.
"I believe the issue is so important not just for airlines, air freight forwarders but for the Hong Kong economy as a whole that some contingency measures should be drawn up," he added.

At 1,377 metres long, it is the world's second longest suspension bridge after the Humber bridge in England, according to the New Airport Projects Coordination Office. Former British prime minister Lady Thatcher will officiate at this week's opening ceremony.
